title: Longer decimal is larger
statement: A decimal with more digits after the point is a larger number, because the digits after the point make a bigger whole number.
example_item: Which is larger, 0.5 or 0.25?
first_source: Resnick, L. B., Nesher, P., Leonard, F., Magone, M., Omanson, S., & Peled, I. (1989). Conceptual bases of arithmetic errors: The case of decimal fractions. Journal for Research in Mathematics Education, 20(1), 8-27.

title: Shorter decimal is larger
statement: A decimal with fewer digits after the point is a larger number, because more digits mean smaller pieces, like a fraction with a bigger denominator.
example_item: Which is larger, 0.85 or 0.8?
first_source: Resnick, L. B., Nesher, P., Leonard, F., Magone, M., Omanson, S., & Peled, I. (1989). Conceptual bases of arithmetic errors: The case of decimal fractions. Journal for Research in Mathematics Education, 20(1), 8-27.

title: Adding fractions across numerators and denominators
statement: Fractions are added by adding the numerators together and adding the denominators together, treating the top and bottom numbers as independent whole numbers, the same way fractions are multiplied.
first_source: Brown, J. S., & VanLehn, K. (1980). Repair theory: A generative theory of bugs in procedural skills. Cognitive Science, 4(4), 379-426.

title: Adding numerators and keeping one denominator
statement: To add fractions you add the numerators and keep the denominator, whichever denominator is written, because the denominator is just a label that does not take part in the sum.
first_source: Ashlock, R. B. (2010). Error Patterns in Computation: Using Error Patterns to Help Each Student Learn (10th ed.). Allyn & Bacon.

title: Adding a whole number to the numerator
statement: To add a whole number and a fraction you add the whole number to the numerator.
first_source: Ashlock, R. B. (2010). Error Patterns in Computation: Using Error Patterns to Help Each Student Learn (10th ed.). Allyn & Bacon.

title: Bigger denominator means bigger fraction
statement: The fraction with the bigger denominator is the bigger fraction, because the denominator is a bigger number.
example_item: Which is larger, 1/3 or 1/8?
first_source: Stafylidou, S., & Vosniadou, S. (2004). The development of students' understanding of the numerical value of fractions. Learning and Instruction, 14(5), 503-518.

title: Cancelling matching digits
statement: A fraction is simplified by crossing out a digit that appears in both the numerator and the denominator.
example_item: Simplify 12/24
first_source: Ashlock, R. B. (2010). Error Patterns in Computation: Using Error Patterns to Help Each Student Learn (10th ed.). Allyn & Bacon.

title: Comparing fractions by the gap between numerator and denominator
statement: The size of a fraction is decided by how many pieces are missing from the whole; fractions with the same gap between numerator and denominator are equal.
example_item: Which is larger, 5/6 or 7/8?
first_source: Pearn, C., & Stephens, M. (2004). Why you have to probe to discover what Year 8 students really think about fractions. In I. Putt, R. Faragher & M. McLean (Eds.), Mathematics Education for the Third Millennium: Towards 2010 (Proceedings of MERGA 27, pp. 430-437). MERGA.

title: Comparing fractions by their whole-number parts
statement: To compare two fractions you compare the numerators and the denominators as whole numbers; a fraction with bigger numbers is a bigger fraction.
example_item: Which is larger, 4/5 or 5/9?
first_source: Obersteiner, A., Van Dooren, W., Van Hoof, J., & Verschaffel, L. (2013). The natural number bias and magnitude representation in fraction comparison by expert mathematicians. Learning and Instruction, 28, 64-72.

title: Cross-multiplying to multiply fractions
statement: To multiply two fractions you multiply diagonally: the first numerator by the second denominator over the first denominator by the second numerator.
first_source: Ashlock, R. B. (2010). Error Patterns in Computation: Using Error Patterns to Help Each Student Learn (10th ed.). Allyn & Bacon.

title: You can only divide a larger number by a smaller one
statement: In a division the bigger number must be divided by the smaller number, so if the divisor is bigger the two numbers should be swapped.
first_source: Fischbein, E., Deri, M., Nello, M. S., & Marino, M. S. (1985). The role of implicit models in solving verbal problems in multiplication and division. Journal for Research in Mathematics Education, 16(1), 3-17.

title: Division always makes smaller
statement: Dividing always gives a result smaller than the number you started with, so dividing by a fraction cannot make a number bigger.
example_item: Without calculating, is 6 / 1/2 more or less than 6?
first_source: Fischbein, E., Deri, M., Nello, M. S., & Marino, M. S. (1985). The role of implicit models in solving verbal problems in multiplication and division. Journal for Research in Mathematics Education, 16(1), 3-17.

title: Division of fractions only means sharing
statement: Dividing means sharing a quantity equally among a number of people, so a division by a fraction has no meaning and must be a mistake or a different operation.
example_item: How many 1/2-cup servings are in 3 cups?
first_source: Fischbein, E., Deri, M., Nello, M. S., & Marino, M. S. (1985). The role of implicit models in solving verbal problems in multiplication and division. Journal for Research in Mathematics Education, 16(1), 3-17.

title: Equivalent fractions by adding the same number
statement: You get an equivalent fraction by adding the same number to the numerator and the denominator, or by subtracting the same number from both.
first_source: Hart, K. M. (Ed.). (1981). Children's Understanding of Mathematics: 11-16. John Murray. (Concepts in Secondary Mathematics and Science project.)

title: Writing a fraction as a decimal by copying its digits
statement: A fraction is written as a decimal by putting its numerator, or its denominator, after the decimal point.
example_item: Write 1/4 as a decimal
first_source: Kerslake, D. (1986). Fractions: Children's Strategies and Errors. NFER-Nelson.

title: A fraction cannot be more than one whole
statement: A fraction is always part of one whole, so the numerator can never be bigger than the denominator and a fraction can never be greater than 1.
first_source: Stafylidou, S., & Vosniadou, S. (2004). The development of students' understanding of the numerical value of fractions. Learning and Instruction, 14(5), 503-518.

title: Inverting both fractions when dividing
statement: To divide fractions you flip both fractions and then multiply.
first_source: Ashlock, R. B. (2010). Error Patterns in Computation: Using Error Patterns to Help Each Student Learn (10th ed.). Allyn & Bacon.

title: Inverting the first fraction when dividing
statement: To divide fractions you flip the first fraction and then multiply.
first_source: Ashlock, R. B. (2010). Error Patterns in Computation: Using Error Patterns to Help Each Student Learn (10th ed.). Allyn & Bacon.

title: Converting a mixed number by adding all its numbers
statement: To write a mixed number as an improper fraction you add the whole number to the numerator and keep the denominator.
example_item: Write 2 1/3 as an improper fraction
first_source: Ashlock, R. B. (2010). Error Patterns in Computation: Using Error Patterns to Help Each Student Learn (10th ed.). Allyn & Bacon.

title: Multiplication always makes bigger
statement: Multiplying always gives a result larger than the number you started with, so multiplying by a fraction cannot make a number smaller.
example_item: Without calculating, is 8 x 3/4 more or less than 8?
first_source: Fischbein, E., Deri, M., Nello, M. S., & Marino, M. S. (1985). The role of implicit models in solving verbal problems in multiplication and division. Journal for Research in Mathematics Education, 16(1), 3-17.

title: Multiplying mixed numbers part by part
statement: To multiply mixed numbers you multiply the whole numbers together and the fractions together and put the two results back together.
first_source: Ashlock, R. B. (2010). Error Patterns in Computation: Using Error Patterns to Help Each Student Learn (10th ed.). Allyn & Bacon.

title: Multiplying needs a common denominator
statement: Before multiplying fractions you must write them with a common denominator, then multiply the numerators and keep the denominator.
first_source: Newton, K. J. (2008). An extensive analysis of preservice elementary teachers' knowledge of fractions. American Educational Research Journal, 45(4), 1080-1110.

title: No number between neighbouring fractions
statement: Fractions come one after another like whole numbers, so between two fractions that are 'next to each other' there is no other number.
example_item: How many numbers are there between 1/5 and 2/5?
first_source: Vamvakoussi, X., & Vosniadou, S. (2004). Understanding the structure of the set of rational numbers: A conceptual change approach. Learning and Instruction, 14(5), 453-467.

title: The whole line is the whole
statement: On a number line the fraction refers to the whole line drawn, so 1/2 is at the middle of the line wherever the line ends.
example_item: Mark 1/2 on a number line from 0 to 3
example_response: at 1 1/2, the middle of the line
first_source: Bright, G. W., Behr, M. J., Post, T. R., & Wachsmuth, I. (1988). Identifying fractions on number lines. Journal for Research in Mathematics Education, 19(3), 215-232.

title: Swapping numerator and denominator when finding a fraction of a quantity
statement: To find a/b of a quantity you divide the quantity by a and multiply by b.
example_item: Find 3/4 of 20
first_source: Hart, K. M. (Ed.). (1981). Children's Understanding of Mathematics: 11-16. John Murray. (Concepts in Secondary Mathematics and Science project.)

title: Writing the shaded part over the unshaded part
statement: A fraction compares the shaded part with the unshaded part, so the number of shaded pieces goes on top and the number of unshaded pieces goes underneath.
example_item: A bar is cut into 5 equal parts and 3 are shaded. What fraction is shaded?
first_source: Hart, K. M. (Ed.). (1981). Children's Understanding of Mathematics: 11-16. John Murray. (Concepts in Secondary Mathematics and Science project.)

title: Subtracting fractions across numerators and denominators
statement: Fractions are subtracted by subtracting the numerators and subtracting the denominators.
first_source: Siegler, R. S., Thompson, C. A., & Schneider, M. (2011). An integrated theory of whole number and fractions development. Cognitive Psychology, 62(4), 273-296.

title: A fraction is two separate whole numbers
statement: A fraction is two whole numbers written one above the other, not a single number with its own size; the numerator and denominator can be read and handled separately.
example_item: Mark 3/4 on a number line from 0 to 10
example_expected: between 0 and 1, three quarters of the way
first_source: Ni, Y., & Zhou, Y.-D. (2005). Teaching and learning fraction and rational numbers: The origins and implications of whole number bias. Educational Psychologist, 40(1), 27-52.

title: Any part of a shape cut into b pieces is 1/b
statement: If a shape is cut into b pieces, each piece is one b-th of the shape, whether or not the pieces are the same size.
example_item: A rectangle is cut into 4 pieces of different sizes; the largest is shaded. What fraction is shaded?
example_expected: Cannot tell from the count; it is more than 1/4
first_source: Kerslake, D. (1986). Fractions: Children's Strategies and Errors. NFER-Nelson.

title: Arrays grow when you add to them
statement: An array gets bigger by itself when you store something past its end, so its size does not need to be decided in advance.
first_source: Chiodini, L., Moreno Santos, I., Gallidabino, A., Tafliovich, A., Santos, A. L., & Hauswirth, M. (2021). A curated inventory of programming language misconceptions. In Proceedings of the 26th ACM Conference on Innovation and Technology in Computer Science Education (ITiCSE '21), 380-386.

title: An array's length is a method call
statement: You get the length of an array by calling a method on it, in the same way as for a string or a list.
example_item: Given int[] a, write an expression for its length.
first_source: Chiodini, L., Moreno Santos, I., Gallidabino, A., Tafliovich, A., Santos, A. L., & Hauswirth, M. (2021). A curated inventory of programming language misconceptions. In Proceedings of the 26th ACM Conference on Innovation and Technology in Computer Science Education (ITiCSE '21), 380-386.

title: A boolean must be compared with true to be used as a condition
statement: A boolean variable or expression cannot be used directly as a condition; it has to be compared with true or false first, and a comparison is the only thing that produces a condition.
example_item: done is a boolean. Write the condition for 'if done'.
first_source: Chiodini, L., Moreno Santos, I., Gallidabino, A., Tafliovich, A., Santos, A. L., & Hauswirth, M. (2021). A curated inventory of programming language misconceptions. In Proceedings of the 26th ACM Conference on Innovation and Technology in Computer Science Education (ITiCSE '21), 380-386.

title: Both operands of and/or are always evaluated
statement: A logical and or or always evaluates both of its operands, whatever the first one turns out to be.
first_source: Chiodini, L., Moreno Santos, I., Gallidabino, A., Tafliovich, A., Santos, A. L., & Hauswirth, M. (2021). A curated inventory of programming language misconceptions. In Proceedings of the 26th ACM Conference on Innovation and Technology in Computer Science Education (ITiCSE '21), 380-386.

title: Both branches of an if-else run in turn
statement: In an if-else statement the if branch runs when the condition is true and then the else branch runs afterwards as well, because it comes next in the code.
first_source: Chiodini, L., Moreno Santos, I., Gallidabino, A., Tafliovich, A., Santos, A. L., & Hauswirth, M. (2021). A curated inventory of programming language misconceptions. In Proceedings of the 26th ACM Conference on Innovation and Technology in Computer Science Education (ITiCSE '21), 380-386.

title: An if statement repeats while its condition holds
statement: The body of an if statement keeps running for as long as the condition is true, like a while loop.
example_item:
x = 0
if x < 3:
    x = x + 1
print(x)
first_source: Chiodini, L., Moreno Santos, I., Gallidabino, A., Tafliovich, A., Santos, A. L., & Hauswirth, M. (2021). A curated inventory of programming language misconceptions. In Proceedings of the 26th ACM Conference on Innovation and Technology in Computer Science Education (ITiCSE '21), 380-386.

title: Variables reset at the start of every loop iteration
statement: Every time a loop body starts again, the variables changed inside it go back to what they were before the loop.
example_item:
total = 0
for n in [1, 2, 3]:
    total = total + n
print(total)
first_source: Chiodini, L., Moreno Santos, I., Gallidabino, A., Tafliovich, A., Santos, A. L., & Hauswirth, M. (2021). A curated inventory of programming language misconceptions. In Proceedings of the 26th ACM Conference on Innovation and Technology in Computer Science Education (ITiCSE '21), 380-386.

title: A while loop stops the instant its condition becomes false
statement: The condition of a while loop is watched continuously, so the loop exits in the middle of the body the moment the condition turns false.
example_item:
i = 0
while i < 2:
    i = i + 1
    print(i)
first_source: Pea, R. D. (1986). Language-independent conceptual "bugs" in novice programming. Journal of Educational Computing Research, 2(1), 25-36.

title: All the statements in a program are active at once
statement: Every line of a program is active at the same time, so a later line can affect what an earlier line did, and a condition anywhere is watched continuously.
example_item:
x = 1
print(x)
x = 2
first_source: Pea, R. D. (1986). Language-independent conceptual "bugs" in novice programming. Journal of Educational Computing Research, 2(1), 25-36.

title: The computer fills in what you meant
statement: The computer understands the purpose of the program and fills in steps that were left out, so a program does what you meant as long as the intention is clear.
example_item:
numbers = [3, 1, 2]
print(numbers)  # print sorted
first_source: Pea, R. D. (1986). Language-independent conceptual "bugs" in novice programming. Journal of Educational Computing Research, 2(1), 25-36.

title: Arguments are matched to parameters by name
statement: The variable passed to a function has to have the same name as the parameter, or the function will not receive it.
example_item:
def show(n):
    print(n)
value = 5
show(value)
first_source: Fleury, A. E. (1991). Parameter passing: The rules the students construct. In Proceedings of the 22nd SIGCSE Technical Symposium on Computer Science Education (SIGCSE '91), 283-286.

title: A recursive function stops by itself
statement: A recursive function stops calling itself when there is nothing left to do, so it does not need an explicit base case.
example_item:
def count_down(n):
    print(n)
    count_down(n - 1)
count_down(3)
example_expected: 3 2 1 0 -1 ... until the recursion limit is hit
first_source: Chiodini, L., Moreno Santos, I., Gallidabino, A., Tafliovich, A., Santos, A. L., & Hauswirth, M. (2021). A curated inventory of programming language misconceptions. In Proceedings of the 26th ACM Conference on Innovation and Technology in Computer Science Education (ITiCSE '21), 380-386.

title: A function can return several separate values
statement: return a, b sends back two separate values, so the caller receives two things rather than one tuple.
example_item:
def f():
    return 1, 2
x = f()
print(type(x))
example_response: int (or 'error, two values into one variable')
first_source: Chiodini, L., Moreno Santos, I., Gallidabino, A., Tafliovich, A., Santos, A. L., & Hauswirth, M. (2021). A curated inventory of programming language misconceptions. In Proceedings of the 26th ACM Conference on Innovation and Technology in Computer Science Education (ITiCSE '21), 380-386.

title: Changing a parameter changes the caller's variable
statement: A parameter is the same variable as the argument that was passed in, so assigning to the parameter inside the function changes the caller's variable, even for numbers and strings.
example_item:
def bump(n):
    n = n + 1
x = 1
bump(x)
print(x)
first_source: Fleury, A. E. (1991). Parameter passing: The rules the students construct. In Proceedings of the 22nd SIGCSE Technical Symposium on Computer Science Education (SIGCSE '91), 283-286.

title: Printing a value is the same as returning it
statement: A function gives its result back by printing it, so a function that prints its answer can be used in an expression, and return is just another way to display.
example_item:
def double(n):
    print(n * 2)
x = double(4)
print(x + 1)
first_source: Sorva, J. (2012). Visual Program Simulation in Introductory Programming Education (Doctoral dissertation, Aalto University). Appendix A catalogues introductory programming misconceptions from the literature.

title: A recursive call jumps back to the start
statement: A recursive call is a jump back to the beginning of the function, using the same variables, so there is only ever one copy of the function running.
first_source: Kahney, H. (1983). What do novice programmers know about recursion? In Proceedings of the SIGCHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems (CHI '83), 235-239.

title: Assigning an object makes a copy
statement: Assigning one object variable to another makes a second, independent copy of the object, so changing one does not affect the other.
example_item:
a = [1, 2]
b = a
b.append(3)
print(a)
first_source: Chiodini, L., Moreno Santos, I., Gallidabino, A., Tafliovich, A., Santos, A. L., & Hauswirth, M. (2021). A curated inventory of programming language misconceptions. In Proceedings of the 26th ACM Conference on Innovation and Technology in Computer Science Education (ITiCSE '21), 380-386.

title: A constant reference means an unchangeable object
statement: Declaring an object variable final or const makes the object it refers to unchangeable, so its fields or elements cannot be modified.
first_source: Chiodini, L., Moreno Santos, I., Gallidabino, A., Tafliovich, A., Santos, A. L., & Hauswirth, M. (2021). A curated inventory of programming language misconceptions. In Proceedings of the 26th ACM Conference on Innovation and Technology in Computer Science Education (ITiCSE '21), 380-386.

title: A constructor must return the object
statement: A constructor creates the object and has to return it at the end, so a constructor without a return statement produces nothing.
example_item: Write a constructor for Point that stores x and y.
example_expected: Point(int x, int y) { this.x = x; this.y = y; }
example_response: Point Point(int x, int y) { this.x = x; this.y = y; return this; }
first_source: Chiodini, L., Moreno Santos, I., Gallidabino, A., Tafliovich, A., Santos, A. L., & Hauswirth, M. (2021). A curated inventory of programming language misconceptions. In Proceedings of the 26th ACM Conference on Innovation and Technology in Computer Science Education (ITiCSE '21), 380-386.

title: == compares the contents of objects
statement: Comparing two object variables with == compares what is inside the objects, so two objects with the same field values are equal.
first_source: Chiodini, L., Moreno Santos, I., Gallidabino, A., Tafliovich, A., Santos, A. L., & Hauswirth, M. (2021). A curated inventory of programming language misconceptions. In Proceedings of the 26th ACM Conference on Innovation and Technology in Computer Science Education (ITiCSE '21), 380-386.

title: A variable contains the whole object
statement: An object variable contains the object itself, not a reference to it, so every variable is its own object and passing it around passes the object.
example_item:
p = Point(1, 2)
q = p
Draw p and q.
example_expected: Two variables, both pointing to one Point object
example_response: Two boxes, each containing a Point(1, 2)
first_source: Chiodini, L., Moreno Santos, I., Gallidabino, A., Tafliovich, A., Santos, A. L., & Hauswirth, M. (2021). A curated inventory of programming language misconceptions. In Proceedings of the 26th ACM Conference on Innovation and Technology in Computer Science Education (ITiCSE '21), 380-386.

title: Plus adds numbers before it concatenates
statement: In an expression that mixes strings and numbers with +, the numbers are added together first and the string is attached afterwards.
example_item: System.out.println("x" + 1 + 2);
first_source: Chiodini, L., Moreno Santos, I., Gallidabino, A., Tafliovich, A., Santos, A. L., & Hauswirth, M. (2021). A curated inventory of programming language misconceptions. In Proceedings of the 26th ACM Conference on Innovation and Technology in Computer Science Education (ITiCSE '21), 380-386.

title: Dividing two integers gives a fraction
statement: Dividing one whole number by another gives the exact mathematical result with a fractional part, whatever the types involved.
example_item:
int x = 7 / 2;
System.out.println(x);
first_source: Qian, Y., & Lehman, J. (2017). Students' misconceptions and other difficulties in introductory programming: A literature review. ACM Transactions on Computing Education, 18(1), Article 1.

title: Assignment states an equation
statement: The equals sign in an assignment states that the two sides are equal, as in algebra, so x = x + 1 is a contradiction and a = b and b = a mean the same thing.
example_item:
x = 5
x = x + 1
What is x?
first_source: du Boulay, B. (1986). Some difficulties of learning to program. Journal of Educational Computing Research, 2(1), 57-73.

title: Assignment links two variables
statement: After a = b the two variables are connected, so whenever b changes later, a changes too.
example_item:
a = 1
b = a
a = 7
What is b?
first_source: Ma, L., Ferguson, J., Roper, M., & Wood, M. (2007). Investigating the viability of mental models held by novice programmers. In Proceedings of the 38th SIGCSE Technical Symposium on Computer Science Education (SIGCSE '07), 499-503.

title: Assignment moves the value out of the source
statement: Assigning a = b moves the value from b into a, so b is empty or zero afterwards.
example_item:
b = 4
a = b
What is b?
first_source: Bayman, P., & Mayer, R. E. (1983). A diagnosis of beginning programmers' misconceptions of BASIC programming statements. Communications of the ACM, 26(9), 677-679.

title: The computer understands variable names
statement: The name of a variable tells the computer what it is for, so a variable called total will add things up and one called largest will hold the biggest value.
example_item:
largest = 0
for n in [4, 9, 2]:
    pass
print(largest)
first_source: Pea, R. D. (1986). Language-independent conceptual "bugs" in novice programming. Journal of Educational Computing Research, 2(1), 25-36.

title: Uninitialised variables start at zero
statement: A variable that has been declared but never assigned holds zero, or an empty value, so it can be safely read or added to.
example_expected: Compile error: count might not have been initialized
first_source: Chiodini, L., Moreno Santos, I., Gallidabino, A., Tafliovich, A., Santos, A. L., & Hauswirth, M. (2021). A curated inventory of programming language misconceptions. In Proceedings of the 26th ACM Conference on Innovation and Technology in Computer Science Education (ITiCSE '21), 380-386.

title: A variable remembers every value it has held
statement: A variable stores every value ever assigned to it, so an earlier value can still be read out later.
example_item:
x = 3
x = 5
print(x)
first_source: du Boulay, B. (1986). Some difficulties of learning to program. Journal of Educational Computing Research, 2(1), 57-73.
